USD.catalyst: The U.S. Dollar Index closed at 102.23, holding above its 20-day (101.14), 50-day (100.09), and 200-day (99.40) simple moving averages as it heads toward a fourth consecutive week of gains despite slipping 0.20% on a one-week G10 composite basis. The greenback continues to draw support from wide short-term yield advantages, including a +144bp SOFR-€STR spread over the euro and a +159bp SOFR-CORRA differential over the Canadian dollar. While softer Nonfarm Payrolls and Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation prints have fueled expectations that the Federal Reserve will pause its tightening cycle at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting, speculative positioning remains heavily skewed in favor of the dollar, evidenced by leveraged funds expanding net-short euro exposure to -82.4k contracts.

GBP.catalyst: The British pound trades with positive momentum, gaining 0.25% across G10 peers over the past week despite closing below its 20-day (1.3295) and 50-day (1.3439) moving averages against the dollar at 1.3234. Sterling has found fundamental backing in hawkish rhetoric from the Bank of England, where Governor Andrew Bailey stressed that monetary policy requires an "unwavering commitment to returning inflation to target" and Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden indicated that further rate increases could be warranted if persistent price pressures mount. Analysts at S&P Global noted that elevated hydrocarbon prices continue to feed headline inflation, projecting an additional 25bp BoE policy tightening later in 2026. Domestic fiscal policy remains the primary upcoming test, with Chancellor attention centered on the UK Autumn Budget scheduled for October 28.

EUR.catalyst: The euro remains heavily pressured across global markets, logging a 0.67% decline on a one-week G10 composite basis and closing below its 20-day (1.1364), 50-day (1.1506), and 200-day (1.1600) moving averages against the dollar at 1.1206. Although Eurostat flash estimates showed September Eurozone headline inflation printing above expectations at 3.8% alongside an 18.8% year-on-year surge in energy costs, dovish commentary from ECB President Christine Lagarde prompted markets to slash October rate hike odds from roughly 75% to 28%. Sentiment is further weighed down by mounting French sovereign debt concerns, even as ECB Governing Council member Martins Kazaks noted that the European economy remains relatively resilient to shocks. Staff growth projections currently anticipate euro area GDP expansion of 0.9% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027.

JPY.catalyst: The Japanese yen continues to underperform its G10 basket, retreating 0.42% on the session and 0.31% over the past week as spot trades at 158.25, below its 200-day moving average of 158.52 against the dollar. Upward pressure on dollar-yen persists due to a +265bp SOFR-TONA carry disadvantage and a deep BoJ-Fed real rate divergence of -2.25% versus +1.63%, compounded by domestic household spending declining for a ninth straight month. However, downside momentum in the yen has been checked by heightened intervention vigilance; official statements confirmed joint US-Japan coordination, with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressing strong support for Tokyo's "decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen." Hawkish remarks from BoJ board member Sato and the Tokyo Financial Exchange's launch of BoJ meeting-by-meeting rate futures have kept markets attentive to near-term policy shifts.

AUD.catalyst: The Australian dollar ranks among the top performers across G10 currencies, posting a composite one-week gain of 0.86% and a daily advance of 0.42%. Spot closed at 0.6986, remaining below its 20-day (0.7033) and 200-day (0.7040) moving averages against the dollar, but finds structural support from a +72bp AONIA-SOFR yield advantage and a +216bp spread over €STR. Market consensus points toward the Reserve Bank of Australia lifting its cash rate from 4.10% to 4.35%, setting it apart as one of the few major central banks extending an active hiking cycle. CFTC positioning shows speculative leveraged funds net long 55.1k contracts, leaving the currency sensitive to broader equity market swings after internal RBA research highlighted that a 20% decline in AI equity valuations could reduce domestic consumer spending by 2.5%.

CAD.catalyst: The Canadian dollar lagged G10 peers with a 0.33% decline over the week and a 0.22% drop on the day, with the greenback pushing to 1.4253 to trade above all major moving averages against the loonie. Sentiment deteriorated sharply following an employment shock that saw the Canadian economy shed 68.3k jobs, expanding the leveraged funds CAD net-short position by 23.4k contracts week-over-week to -72.5k contracts. The widening labor slack reinforces a +159bp SOFR-CORRA carry penalty that disfavors the loonie against U.S. fixed-income benchmarks. Although the Bank of Canada faces a severe growth downshift, Royal Bank of Canada strategists anticipate gradual economic improvement over the medium term.

CHF.catalyst: The Swiss franc demonstrated modest stability across the G10 complex, posting a composite daily gain of 0.13% while spot closed at 0.8300, holding above its 20-day (0.8273) and 50-day (0.8160) moving averages against the dollar. The currency continues to benefit from regional flight-to-safety flows triggered by escalating French fiscal debt distress. Domestically, the Swiss National Bank and the Federal Reserve both head into scheduled rate decisions next week, with SNB policymakers broadly expected to hold borrowing costs steady. Market participants are monitoring the tone of incoming central bank communications, particularly regarding external trade and inflation pass-through, while institutional integration advances following the SNB's participation in Project Agora's cross-border tokenization testing.

Strategists at MUFG warned that high-beta currencies face vulnerability in an environment of elevated global yields, which could lead the kiwi to underperform over the coming months. Offsetting these external crosswinds are persistent domestic interest rate expectations, with markets pricing the possibility that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will deliver an Official Cash Rate increase at its upcoming October 28 meeting.

NOK.catalyst: The Norwegian krone gained 0.99% across G10 currencies over the past week, supported by the Norges Bank maintaining its benchmark policy rate at 4.25%. Spot against the dollar closed at 9.5500, positioning above its 20-day (9.502) and 200-day (9.546) moving averages. UBS highlighted the currency's attractive yield profile, noting that krone carry positions remain favored among European crosses given the central bank's firm stance against sticky underlying price pressures. In her recent autumn lecture, Norges Bank Governor Ida Wolden Bache addressed why the last mile of disinflation is taking longer than anticipated, reinforcing expectations that Norwegian interest rates will stay higher for longer.

SEK.catalyst: The Swedish krona gained 0.69% over the past week against its G10 basket, though it pulled back 0.21% on the session, with spot closing against the dollar at 9.9920, above its 20-day moving average of 9.9210. Underpinning the currency's weekly resilience, Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen signaled potential grounds for policy tightening, pointing to stronger-than-expected domestic economic growth and persistent upside inflation risks. However, broader upside remains restrained by external interest rate dynamics; UBS strategists Clémence Dumoncel maintained a EUR/SEK forecast of 11.00 for December 2026, noting that elevated global benchmark yields will continue to constrain krona outperformance despite robust domestic macro fundamentals.
